free.title: 6-DAY RAINY ESCAPE
free.caption:
RAINY DAY · BATTERY PARK CITY

It's raining across NYC today, so skip the umbrella and walk into 16 real palm trees instead. The Winter Garden at Brookfield Place is a free, 24/7 glass atrium in Battery Park City that turns any gray Sunday into a mini escape.

The barrel-vault glass roof was rebuilt in 2002 after 9/11 damage, and the palms inside have been growing here for decades - each one climbs about six inches a year. Marble floors, free wifi, and floor-to-ceiling views of North Cove Marina make this one of downtown's most overlooked rainy-day spots, and most tourists walk right past it on their way to the Oculus.

Best light hits around 4-6pm, when the low sun turns the whole atrium gold. Hudson Eats food hall is one floor up if you want to turn this into a full afternoon.

Send this to whoever's stuck inside with you today.

food.title: DEKALB MARKET HALL
food.caption:
FOOD & MARKET · DOWNTOWN BROOKLYN

Raining all day in NYC, so here's the move: DeKalb Market Hall in Downtown Brooklyn, a food hall packed under one roof at City Point with more than 40 vendors and zero reason to go outside.

It opens at 11am (8am for breakfast vendors) and runs until 10pm every single day, with seating for 500+ people so you're not standing around with a tray. The lineup covers just about every cuisine in one building, which makes it an easy pick when the whole group can't agree on food.

Go before noon or after 3pm if you want to dodge the lunch rush, and split plates across a few stalls instead of committing to just one.

Send this to your rainy Sunday food crew.

art.title: 6 SECRETS OF THE FLATIRON BUILDING
art.caption:
HIDDEN GEM · FLATIRON DISTRICT

You've walked past the Flatiron Building a hundred times, but here are 6 things most New Yorkers don't know about the wedge-shaped landmark where Fifth Avenue crosses Broadway at 23rd St.

It wasn't even called Flatiron at first - the official name was the Fuller Building, after the developer who commissioned it, and the public nickname just stuck. At its narrowest point the triangular prow is only about 6 feet wide, and back in 1902 critics were so sure the whole thing would topple in the wind that engineers built the steel frame to handle four times the expected load. The wind was real, too: gusts whipping around the corner became local legend and helped coin the old New York phrase "23 skidoo."

Best photo spot is the traffic island at 23rd and Broadway, and it looks even better lit gold at sunset.

Send this to whoever always walks past without looking up.
